The net reactance is 62.8 minus 159.2, which is minus 96.4 ohms, so the circuit is net capacitive at this frequency, dominated by the capacitor because the frequency is below resonance. The impedance is 50 - j96.4, with magnitude the square root of 2500 plus 9293, about 108.6 ohms, at an angle of arctangent(-96.4/50), about minus 62.6 degrees. The current is 10 divided by 108.6, about 92.1 milliamps, leading the source voltage by 62.6 degrees. The individual component voltages follow from multiplying that current by each impedance: 4.6 volts across the resistor, in phase with the current; 5.79 volts across the inductor, leading the current by 90 degrees; and 14.66 volts across the capacitor, lagging by 90 degrees. Those three numbers, 4.6, 5.79 and 14.66, sum arithmetically to 25.05 volts, which is two and a half times the 10-volt source. Nothing is wrong. They must be added as phasors, and because the inductor and capacitor voltages are exactly 180 degrees apart they partly cancel, leaving a net reactive voltage of 14.66 minus 5.79, or 8.87 volts, at right angles to the resistor's 4.6 volts. The square root of 4.6 squared plus 8.87 squared is 9.99 volts, the source voltage, as Kirchhoff's law demands. This is the single most important lesson of alternating-current work and the one that most often catches out a beginner with a multimeter. Component voltages in a reactive circuit do not add arithmetically, and individual reactive voltages can substantially exceed the supply. Near resonance the excess becomes extreme, and a capacitor rated comfortably for the supply voltage can be destroyed by the voltage that appears across it. Sweeping the frequency reveals the full character of the circuit. Well below 1592 hertz the capacitive term grows without bound and the current tends to zero: the capacitor is blocking. Well above it the inductive term dominates and the current again falls: the inductor is choking. At exactly the frequency where the two match, the reactance vanishes altogether. The impedance curve is therefore a V, with a floor equal to R, and the phase swings from nearly plus 90 degrees of current lead at low frequency, through zero at the bottom of the V, to nearly 90 degrees of lag at high frequency. Every property of a tuned circuit is contained in that single picture.

sections.heading: Real Power, Reactive Power and Power Factor
sections.body: Because voltage and current are generally out of step, calculating power in an alternating circuit requires more care than multiplying two meter readings. Instantaneous power is always the product of instantaneous voltage and current, but when they are out of phase that product is negative during part of each cycle, meaning energy is flowing back from the circuit to the source. Averaging over a cycle gives the real power P = V*I*cos(phi), measured in watts, where V and I are RMS values and phi is the phase angle between them. The factor cos(phi) is the power factor. Only real power does useful work or produces heat, and only real power is billed to a domestic customer. The product V*I without the cosine is the apparent power S, measured in volt-amperes rather than watts to keep the distinction visible. It represents what the wires, transformers and switchgear must actually carry. The remaining component, Q = V*I*sin(phi), is the reactive power, measured in volt-amperes reactive, or VAR. It represents energy shuttling back and forth between the source and the circuit's magnetic and electric fields, doing no net work but consuming conductor capacity and causing real resistive losses along the way. The three relate as a right triangle, S squared equals P squared plus Q squared, and the whole picture is often drawn as the power triangle. A concrete illustration shows why utilities care. An industrial motor drawing 100 amps at 400 volts with a power factor of 0.7 lagging, typical of a lightly loaded induction motor, has an apparent power of 40 kilovolt-amperes but a real power of only 28 kilowatts. The cabling and transformer must be sized for 100 amps while the customer's useful work corresponds to only 70. The resistive losses in the supply network go as current squared, so the wasted heat is roughly double what it would be at unity power factor. Large consumers are therefore billed on apparent power or penalised for poor power factor. Correction is straightforward in principle. Since inductive loads make current lag and capacitors make it lead, connecting the right capacitance in parallel with an inductive load supplies the reactive power locally, so it circulates between load and capacitor rather than travelling back down the supply line. Correcting the motor above from 0.7 to 0.95 requires about 19.4 kilovolt-amperes reactive of capacitance, and reduces the line current from 100 amps to about 74. The subtlety worth flagging is that on modern loads with non-sinusoidal currents, such as switch-mode supplies and variable-speed drives, the displacement power factor described here is only part of the story; harmonic distortion also degrades the true power factor, and naively adding capacitors to such a system can excite a resonance and make matters considerably worse.

sections.heading: Frequency Response, Decibels and Bode Plots
sections.body: Because impedance depends on frequency, so does the behaviour of any circuit containing reactance. The natural way to describe that behaviour is the transfer function, written H(j*omega), defined as the output phasor divided by the input phasor. Being complex, it has a magnitude, telling how much the circuit scales the signal, and an angle, telling how much it shifts the timing. Plotting both against frequency characterises the circuit completely, at least for linear operation. The standard presentation, introduced by Hendrik Bode at Bell Labs in the 1930s and 1940s, uses logarithmic axes for both frequency and magnitude. Frequency runs logarithmically because circuits of interest span many orders of magnitude and because equal ratios of frequency, an octave being a factor of two and a decade a factor of ten, produce equal effects. Magnitude is expressed in decibels, computed as 20 times the base-ten logarithm of the voltage ratio. The factor of 20 rather than 10 appears because the decibel is fundamentally a power ratio and power goes as voltage squared. Useful landmarks: a voltage ratio of 2 is about 6 dB, a ratio of 10 is exactly 20 dB, a ratio of 0.707 is minus 3 dB, and a ratio of 0.5 is minus 6 dB. Consider the simplest possible case, a resistor in series with a capacitor with the output taken across the capacitor. Applying the voltage divider with complex impedances gives H = (1/(j*omega*C)) divided by (R + 1/(j*omega*C)), which simplifies to 1/(1 + j*omega*R*C). At very low frequency the term j*omega*R*C is negligible, H is approximately 1, and the output equals the input. At very high frequency that term dominates and the magnitude falls as 1 over omega*R*C, which on logarithmic axes is a straight line descending at 20 dB per decade, equivalently 6 dB per octave. The two straight-line asymptotes meet where omega*R*C equals 1, defining the corner or cutoff frequency, fc = 1/(2*pi*R*C). At that frequency the actual magnitude is 1 over the square root of 2, exactly minus 3 dB, and the output power is half the input power, which is why it is also called the half-power point. Phase tells a parallel story that is often more revealing. At low frequency the phase shift is zero, at the corner it is exactly minus 45 degrees, and far above it approaches minus 90 degrees, with the transition spread over about two decades. For a 10-kilohm resistor and a 15.9-nanofarad capacitor the corner sits at 1 kilohertz. This asymptotic sketching method is what makes Bode plots so useful in practice: a competent engineer can draw a usable frequency response for a moderately complex network in a minute, without computing a single point, simply by locating the corner frequencies and adding slopes.

sections.heading: Filters: Shaping the Spectrum
sections.body: A filter is any circuit whose transfer function deliberately favours some frequencies over others, and the simplest useful ones are two-component dividers. Swapping which element the output is taken across inverts the behaviour. Resistor in series with capacitor, output across the capacitor, gives a low-pass response: low frequencies pass, high frequencies are attenuated, because the capacitor's impedance falls with frequency and progressively shorts the output. Take the output across the resistor instead and the same two components form a high-pass filter. The corner frequency, 1/(2*pi*R*C), is identical either way. The same pair of possibilities exists for a resistor and inductor, with the roles reversed and the corner at R/(2*pi*L). These first-order filters have gentle skirts, rolling off at 20 dB per decade, which is often inadequate. Cascading sections steepens the slope by 20 dB per decade for each additional reactive element, but naively cascading two RC sections does not simply double the response, because the second section loads the first. Either the sections must be separated by a buffer amplifier or the loading must be accounted for, which is one reason active filters using operational amplifiers became standard. Combining an inductor and a capacitor gives a second-order response with a 40 dB per decade slope from just two reactive components, and additionally allows a peak near the corner. Beyond simple low-pass and high-pass lie two further shapes. A band-pass filter passes a band and rejects everything outside it, and can be built as a series LC in the signal path, whose impedance is minimum at resonance, or as a cascade of a high-pass and a low-pass with the high-pass corner below the low-pass corner. A band-stop or notch filter does the reverse, and is the tool of choice for removing a single interfering frequency such as 50-hertz mains hum from an instrumentation signal. Real filter design involves trade-offs that have been formalised into named families, each optimising something different at the expense of something else. The Butterworth response, described by Stephen Butterworth in 1930, is maximally flat in the passband with a moderate transition. The Chebyshev response achieves a steeper transition by tolerating ripple in the passband, with more ripple buying more steepness. The elliptic or Cauer response is steeper still, with ripple in both passband and stopband. The Bessel response sacrifices steepness for a maximally linear phase, meaning all frequencies are delayed equally, which preserves the shape of pulses and matters greatly in data and video work. No family is best; they trade amplitude flatness, transition steepness and phase linearity against each other, and choosing among them is the substance of filter design. One practical warning applies to all of them. A filter's published response assumes specified source and load impedances, and connecting one between arbitrary impedances shifts the corner frequency and can destroy the shape entirely. A passive LC filter designed for 50 ohms at both ends will misbehave badly if driven from a high-impedance source or loaded by an open circuit, which is a common and puzzling bench failure.

sections.heading: Series Resonance: When the Reactances Cancel
sections.body: Something remarkable happens to a series RLC circuit at the one frequency where the inductive and capacitive reactances are exactly equal in magnitude. Since they are opposite in sign, they cancel completely, the impedance collapses to the resistance alone, and the circuit behaves for that one frequency as if the inductor and capacitor were not there. Setting omega*L equal to 1/(omega*C) and solving gives the resonant angular frequency omega0 = 1/sqrt(L*C), or in hertz, f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)). Notably the resistance does not appear: resonant frequency depends only on the inductance and capacitance. For the earlier example, L = 10 millihenries and C = 1 microfarad, the product L*C is 1e-8, its square root is 1e-4, and f0 = 1/(2*pi*1e-4), about 1592 hertz. At that frequency the impedance falls from the 108.6 ohms computed at 1 kilohertz to just the 50-ohm resistance, and the current rises from 92 milliamps to 200 milliamps, in phase with the source. A series resonant circuit is a frequency-selective short circuit. The dramatic part is what appears across the individual reactive components. At resonance the inductive reactance is 2*pi*1592*0.01, about 100 ohms. The 200-milliamp current through it produces 20 volts, and the same 20 volts appears across the capacitor with the opposite phase. The source is 10 volts. Twice the supply voltage stands across each reactive component, and they cancel exactly so Kirchhoff's law is satisfied. This voltage magnification factor is the quality factor, Q, and for a series circuit Q = omega0*L/R, equivalently (1/R)*sqrt(L/C). Here Q is 100/50, which is 2. With a higher Q the effect becomes spectacular and hazardous. Reduce the resistance to 1 ohm and Q becomes 100, so a 10-volt source produces a kilovolt across the capacitor. This is not a curiosity; it is the operating principle of the induction coil, of Tesla coils, and of the tuned input of a radio receiver, where a microvolt of antenna signal is magnified by a Q of a few hundred before amplification. It is also a genuine failure mode in power systems, where a resonance between line inductance and power-factor-correction capacitance, excited by a harmonic from a variable-speed drive, has destroyed capacitor banks. Q also determines selectivity. The bandwidth, defined between the two frequencies at which the current falls to 0.707 of its peak, is BW = f0/Q. A Q of 2 at 1592 hertz gives a 796-hertz bandwidth, which is very broad; a Q of 100 gives 15.9 hertz, sharp enough to separate adjacent broadcast stations. High Q means narrow, selective and strongly magnifying; low Q means broad, tolerant and gentle. Two design consequences follow directly. Because f0 depends on the product L*C but Q depends on the ratio of L to C, the same resonant frequency can be reached with many combinations, and the choice sets the impedance level and the achievable Q. A large inductor with a small capacitor gives a high-impedance, high-Q circuit; the reverse gives a low-impedance, heavily damped one. And because resistance alone sets Q while leaving f0 untouched, tuning and damping can be adjusted independently, which is exactly what makes the topology so tractable in design.

sections.heading: Parallel Resonance and the Tank Circuit
sections.body: Placing the inductor and capacitor in parallel rather than in series produces the mirror image: at resonance the impedance reaches a maximum rather than a minimum. The circuit is called a tank because energy sloshes back and forth between the magnetic field of the coil and the electric field of the capacitor, much as liquid oscillates in a vessel, with the external source needing to supply only the losses. The mechanism is best seen in admittances, which add for parallel elements. The capacitor's admittance is j*omega*C and the inductor's is 1/(j*omega*L), which is minus j/(omega*L). At the frequency where omega*C equals 1/(omega*L) they cancel, the total admittance of the reactive pair is zero, and the impedance is therefore infinite for an ideal lossless pair. The resonant frequency is the same expression as before, f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)). Physically, large equal and opposite currents circulate around the loop between inductor and capacitor while almost no current is drawn from the source. In a series circuit Q magnifies voltage; in a parallel circuit Q magnifies current, and the circulating current is Q times the supply current. Real components have losses, overwhelmingly the winding resistance of the inductor, and this makes the peak impedance finite. The standard model places a small resistance r in series with L, and the resulting peak impedance, called the dynamic resistance, works out to approximately L/(C*r), which can also be written as Q*omega0*L or Q squared times r. For a 100-microhenry coil with 2 ohms of series resistance resonating with 250 picofarads at about 1 megahertz, the dynamic resistance is 100e-6 divided by (250e-12 times 2), which is 200 kilohms. A circuit built from a coil of 2 ohms presents 200 kilohms at one specific frequency and a few ohms everywhere else. That astonishing selectivity is why the parallel tank is the collector load in every traditional radio-frequency amplifier and the frequency-determining element in most oscillators. An important practical note is that a real inductor's Q is almost always the limiting factor. Capacitors of good dielectric routinely achieve Q values in the thousands, while a wound air-cored coil at a few megahertz might reach 200 and a small ferrite-cored one considerably less. Coil Q also varies strongly with frequency, rising initially and then falling as skin effect, proximity effect and core losses take over. When a resonant circuit underperforms, the inductor is the first suspect. Where very high Q is required, resonators of an entirely different physical kind are used instead: quartz crystals achieve Q values of 10,000 to over a million, which is why they, and not LC circuits, set the frequency of clocks and radio transmitters. A further practical consequence is that whatever the tank is connected to also loads it, so the loaded Q of a tank feeding a following stage is always lower than its unloaded Q, sometimes by a large factor.

sections.heading: Q, Bandwidth and Damping as One Idea
sections.body: The quality factor turns up in so many guises that it is worth assembling them into a single picture, because they are all the same number seen from different directions. Its most fundamental definition is energetic: Q equals 2*pi times the energy stored in the resonator divided by the energy dissipated per cycle. A resonator with Q of 100 loses about one sixty-third of its stored energy each cycle, since dividing by 2*pi turns the per-cycle fractional loss into 1/Q. This definition applies equally to an electrical tuned circuit, a pendulum, a tuning fork, a church bell, a quartz crystal and an optical cavity, and the numbers are instructive: a car suspension has a Q below 1 by design, a pendulum clock perhaps 10,000, a quartz watch crystal around 100,000, and the mirrors of a gravitational-wave detector far higher still. Its second face is the frequency-domain one: Q equals the resonant frequency divided by the half-power bandwidth, so a 10-megahertz circuit with Q of 50 has a 200-kilohertz bandwidth. Sharpness of tuning and lowness of loss are the same property. This is why a receiver cannot be made arbitrarily selective without consequence; narrowing the bandwidth to reject an adjacent station eventually starts to remove the sidebands carrying the wanted signal's information. Its third face is in the time domain. Struck with an impulse rather than driven with a sinusoid, a resonant circuit rings at approximately its resonant frequency with an amplitude decaying exponentially, and the number of cycles before the amplitude falls to about four per cent of its initial value is roughly Q. Control engineers prefer the reciprocal-like quantity called the damping ratio, zeta, related by zeta = 1/(2Q). A damping ratio below 1 gives an underdamped, ringing response; exactly 1 is critical damping, the fastest approach to the final value without overshoot; above 1 is overdamped and sluggish. A series RLC with R equal to twice the square root of L over C is critically damped, and this is precisely the calculation behind choosing a damping resistor to stop a relay driver or a probe compensation network from ringing. Seeing these as one idea pays off constantly. If a filter rings on a step input, its Q is too high, and the remedy is more loss. If an oscillator drifts or is noisy, its resonator Q is too low, and the remedy is a better resonator. If a tuned amplifier is too broad, adding a resistor deliberately across the tank will broaden it further in a controlled way, a technique called damping or loading, used routinely to flatten the response of intermediate-frequency stages at the cost of gain.

sections.heading: Real Components Are Not Ideal
sections.body: Every calculation above treats resistors, capacitors and inductors as pure. Real components are each a small network, and above a certain frequency the parasitic elements dominate the intended one. Ignoring this is the most common reason a design that simulates perfectly fails on the bench. A real capacitor has equivalent series resistance, arising from lead resistance, plate resistance and dielectric loss, and equivalent series inductance from its leads and internal geometry. The series inductance means every capacitor is itself a series resonant circuit with a self-resonant frequency, above which it behaves as an inductor. A through-hole 100-nanofarad ceramic capacitor with roughly 10 nanohenries of lead inductance self-resonates near 5 megahertz; a surface-mount version of the same value in an 0402 package, with perhaps 0.6 nanohenries, self-resonates above 20 megahertz. This is the real reason decoupling capacitors must be small packages placed close to the pin, and why several values in parallel are sometimes used, though that practice can create an anti-resonance between them that is worse than either alone. Electrolytic capacitors have comparatively enormous equivalent series resistance, often an ohm or more, which both limits their usefulness at frequency and causes them to heat internally under ripple current, the dominant failure mechanism in switching power supplies. A real inductor has winding resistance, which rises with frequency because of skin effect: alternating current crowds into a surface layer whose depth is about 66 micrometres in copper at 1 megahertz and 2.1 millimetres at 1 kilohertz, so above a few hundred kilohertz the interior of a thick wire carries almost nothing. It also has inter-winding capacitance, giving it too a self-resonant frequency above which it behaves as a capacitor, and if it has a magnetic core it has hysteresis and eddy-current losses that grow with frequency and flux and can drive the core into saturation, at which point the inductance collapses abruptly and non-linearly. Even a resistor is imperfect: wirewound types are frankly inductive, and any component's leads contribute roughly a nanohenry per millimetre. Beyond components, the circuit itself becomes a component. Once a conductor is a significant fraction of a wavelength, typically taken as more than about a twentieth, lumped analysis fails entirely and transmission-line theory with its characteristic impedance, reflections and standing waves must be used. A wavelength in free space is 300 metres at 1 megahertz but only 30 centimetres at 1 gigahertz, so a three-centimetre track is negligible in the first case and a significant transmission line in the second. Signals on a printed circuit board travel at roughly half to two-thirds the speed of light depending on the dielectric, which shortens the wavelength and brings the threshold closer than the free-space figure suggests. The practical discipline that follows is to know each component's self-resonant frequency and to stay well below it where the component is meant to behave as its nominal type. Manufacturers publish impedance-versus-frequency curves for exactly this purpose, and reading them is far more informative than reading the marked value. Much of what looks like mysterious high-frequency misbehaviour is simply a parasitic that was never on the schematic.

sections.heading: Measuring Impedance and Finding Resonance on the Bench
sections.body: Calculated values and real ones diverge, so measurement matters. The following procedure finds the actual resonant frequency and loaded Q of an LC circuit using ordinary equipment, and needs no specialist analyser. The principle is that a series resonant circuit's impedance dips to a minimum at resonance, so if it is fed through a known series resistor, the voltage across the resonant pair reaches a minimum, or across the resistor a maximum, at f0.
ingredients: A signal generator with a calibrated frequency readout, ideally sine output with adjustable amplitude; a cheap DDS module covering 1 hertz to a few megahertz is entirely adequate for audio and low radio-frequency work.
An oscilloscope, preferably dual channel so source and response can be compared directly, or an AC millivoltmeter if only magnitude is needed.
A known series resistor, typically 47 to 100 ohms, of 1 per cent tolerance, measured beforehand with a good ohmmeter.
The inductor and capacitor under test, plus a short length of wire and a solderless breadboard or, better at higher frequencies, a small piece of copper-clad board for a ground plane.
A frequency counter if the generator's own readout is not trustworthy; many inexpensive generators are several per cent out.
A x10 oscilloscope probe, which loads the circuit far less than a x1 probe.
steps: Measure the components individually first if you can, and note that a capacitor's marked value may be 20 per cent out and an inductor's more. Compute the expected resonant frequency from f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)) so you know roughly where to look.

Wire the generator output through the known resistor into the series combination of L and C, with the far end returned to the generator ground. Keep the leads short, since stray inductance and capacitance shift the result.
Connect one oscilloscope channel across the generator output and the other across the resistor. The voltage across the resistor is proportional to the current through the circuit.

Set the generator to a modest amplitude, a volt or so peak-to-peak, and sweep slowly through the expected frequency, watching the resistor voltage. Adjust the generator amplitude as you go if its output is not flat with frequency, keeping the source constant.

Find the frequency of maximum resistor voltage. That is the true series resonant frequency f0. If it differs from the calculation by more than a few per cent, suspect the capacitor's tolerance or stray capacitance first.

Confirm resonance independently by checking phase: at f0 the current is exactly in phase with the source voltage, which on a dual-trace display means the two waveforms cross zero together, and on an X-Y display collapses the ellipse to a straight line.
Note the peak voltage, then find the two frequencies above and below at which it falls to 0.707 of that peak. Their difference is the bandwidth, and Q equals f0 divided by that bandwidth.

Remember that the measured Q is the loaded Q, degraded by your series resistor and by the probe. To estimate the component Q, repeat with a smaller series resistor and see how the figure changes; if it keeps rising, your measurement, not the circuit, is the limit.

sections.heading: Where the Method Breaks Down
sections.body: Phasor analysis is powerful precisely because it makes strong assumptions, and every one of those assumptions is a boundary beyond which the answers stop being trustworthy. Knowing where the boundaries lie is as important as knowing the technique. The first and most important assumption is linearity. Phasors require that doubling the input doubles the output and that superposition holds. Diodes, transistors driven beyond their small-signal range, saturating magnetic cores, and any component whose value changes with the applied voltage all violate this. Class II ceramic capacitors, the X5R and X7R dielectrics that dominate modern designs, can lose more than half their marked capacitance at their rated DC bias, which quietly shifts every corner and resonant frequency computed from the nameplate value. In a non-linear circuit, a sinusoidal input produces an output containing harmonics that were not present at the input, and the whole conceptual apparatus of a single-frequency impedance no longer applies. The usual remedy is to linearise about an operating point and analyse small signals, accepting that the result is valid only for small excursions. The second assumption is time-invariance. If component values change during the analysis, as in a switching converter where transistors reconfigure the topology tens of thousands of times a second, there is no single impedance to speak of. Such circuits are handled by averaging techniques or by simulation in the time domain. The third is the steady state. Phasors describe what happens after all transients have died away, which for a circuit of Q around 100 means many hundreds of cycles. They say nothing about switch-on surges, the inrush current of a transformer energised at the wrong point in the cycle, or the ringing that follows a step. Those require time-domain analysis, whether by differential equation, Laplace transform or simulation. The fourth is the single frequency. A distorted waveform must be decomposed into its Fourier components, each analysed separately at its own impedance, and the results recombined. This is not merely academic: harmonic currents from non-linear loads flow through impedances that rise with frequency, so the third and fifth harmonics of a 50-hertz supply can cause overheating in transformers and, in three-phase systems, dangerous currents in a neutral conductor sized on the assumption that the phases would cancel. Finally, a safety note that follows directly from resonance. Reactive voltage magnification is real, and a circuit fed from a modest supply can develop lethal or destructive voltages across an inductor or capacitor near resonance. Rate components for the voltage that will actually appear across them, not for the supply voltage, and treat any resonant circuit connected to the mains, whether deliberately or accidentally through power-factor capacitors, as capable of surprising you.
